status: PROPOSAL — staged. Erik: 'we should look for corollaries to this mechanic.'

thePattern.name: THE VESSEL
thePattern.shape: A craft that STORES its tradition's own medium over time, can be FED faster by spending energy, and ABSORBS incoming damage of that same type as fuel. Three properties, one idea: a thing that holds your element is also fed by your element and defended against your element.
thePattern.whyItGeneralises: ⚠️ IT IS ALREADY IN THE GAME ON THE OTHER SIDE. `absorb` is an authored affinity verdict, and `the_bright_devourer` ABSORBS LIGHT — a creature that eats the thing aimed at it. The vessel pattern is that mechanic handed to players, and the engine already resolves it.
thePattern.theConstraint: ⚠️ IT MUST ANSWER ONLY ONE TYPE. A vessel that drinks everything is armour and strictly better than a shield. A vessel that drinks LIGHT is a counter — brilliant against a Radiant, useless against an edge, and that asymmetry is the whole design.

corollaries.note: fed by any light craft; absorbs light damage; never idle because it fills at a rate

corollaries.how: A chord that HOLDS. Fed by another harmonic playing into it — two singers fill it far faster than one, exactly as with two Radiants. Absorbs SOUND damage: `sonic_resonance` aimed at the bearer is taken into the chord instead of into the chest. ⚠️ AND IT HAS A COST THE WELL DOES NOT — a chord that is holding is AUDIBLE, so a harmonic carrying a full one cannot be quiet.

A held threshold that banks decay rather than light. Fed by an ashwarden spending into it; absorbs DECAY damage aimed at the bearer. ⚠️ ITS COST IS THE BEST OF THE SET: what it banks is still decay, and a full one has to be SPENT OR IT SPOILS — an Ashwarden carrying a charged vessel is carrying a deadline.

Banked growth, fed by tending. Absorbs LIVING damage — the_forced_bloom turned on the bearer feeds them instead. ⚠️ INVERTED COST: it does not spoil, it OVERGROWS. A rootkin who over-fills a vessel gets the_forced_bloom's problem on themselves.

Mechanically it fits — a held-open aperture could bank precursor force and drink precursor damage. BUT `hold_the_aperture` is authored as costing continuously and being 'the hardest thing in the game'. Making it also a battery makes the hardest thing in the game PROFITABLE. Flagging it as the corollary I am declining, because the pattern fitting is not a reason to apply it.

A harbor that drinks shadow would make umbral the hard counter to itself, which is thematically sharp — the Smotherers' own craft turned aside. Worth Erik's call, since it makes umbral-vs-umbral the most defensive matchup in the game.

whatToBuildFirst: THE HARMONIC CHORD. It is the closest corollary, its cost (a holding chord is AUDIBLE) is genuinely different from the Well's, and it proves the pattern travels — one instance is a craft, two is a mechanic.
openForErik: the precursor one I declined — agree, or is a profitable aperture interesting?
the umbral one changes what umbral IS in a fight; worth doing?
should a vessel be TAKEABLE? a charged Well is loot, and a full one is worth a great deal — that is either a good hook or a griefing problem

theFourProperties.note: ⚠️ ERIK COMPLETED THE PATTERN. A vessel is not three properties, it is SIX, and the last three are what make it a risk rather than free storage.
theFourProperties.1_stores: holds its tradition's medium, filling at a rate
theFourProperties.2_fedByCraft: another practitioner can spend energy into it to fill it faster
theFourProperties.3_absorbs: drinks incoming damage OF ITS OWN TYPE ONLY, converting harm to charge
theFourProperties.4_capacity: ⚠️ a hard ceiling, equal to the rank's prep cost — a vessel holds exactly what it took to fill
theFourProperties.5_overcharge: ⚠️ past capacity it WARNS, then fails — and each medium fails in ITS OWN WAY
theFourProperties.6_venting: ⚠️ the excess can be tapped and aimed instead, which turns overcharge from a punishment into a DECISION UNDER PRESSURE
theFourProperties.7_takeable: a charged vessel can be carried off — and a thief who does not know the capacity is carrying a bomb

overchargeByMedium.note: ⚠️ THE BEST PART OF ERIK'S ADDITION: every element fails differently, so the same mechanic produces five completely different scenes. None of these is 'it explodes' with a reskin.

light.fails: BURSTS — 6d6 to everyone WITHIN SIGHT, blinding them for the scene
light.counterplay: opaque cover, because it travels by sight rather than by radius

sound.fails: SHATTERS — everything brittle nearby breaks, and the bearer's hearing goes first
sound.counterplay: distance and soft ground; and the chord was audible the whole time, so it is the one overcharge everyone SAW coming
sound.plainly: When it bursts, everything brittle within earshot breaks — glass, ceramic, bone at 3d6 — and the bearer is deafened for a day, taking a penalty to anything needing hearing.

decay.fails: ⚠️ BLOOMS — the banked rot does not detonate, it SPREADS, and keeps spreading until something stops it
decay.counterplay: it is slow, so it is answerable — but by then it is a place with a problem rather than a moment with one
decay.plainly: When it bursts, the banked rot enters the ground and spreads outward one zone per day, spoiling food, water and worked material as it goes. It does not stop on its own; it stops when someone with a decay craft or enough labour halts it. Nothing takes damage at the moment it bursts.

living.fails: OVERGROWS INTO THE NEAREST LIVING THING
living.plainly: When it bursts, the banked growth takes the single nearest living creature and forces growth into it for 5d6 living damage, continuing at 1d6 per round until that creature dies or the charge is used up. The bearer is usually nearest, so the bearer is usually the target.
living.targetRule: the nearest living creature by distance, measured from the vessel. Ties resolve toward the bearer.
living.whatCountsAsLiving: any creature. ⚠️ PLANTS DO NOT COUNT — the growth wants something that can be grown PAST its shape, and a tree has no shape to exceed. This is why a rootkin cannot simply stand in a forest.
living.counterplay: ⚠️ THE ONLY WAY TO NOT BE THE TARGET IS FOR ANOTHER CREATURE TO BE CLOSER TO THE VESSEL THAN YOU ARE. Set the vessel down and walk away and it takes whatever wanders near — livestock, a companion animal, a person. Hold it and it takes you. THERE IS NO OPTION WHERE NOTHING IS HURT, which is the point: the rootkin overcharge is the only one in the set whose counterplay is DECIDING WHO INSTEAD OF YOU.
living.andTheVentIsDifferentToo: venting a living overcharge does not fire it outward — it puts the growth into something ON PURPOSE. A rootkin who vents well heals a field or a herd; one who vents badly has still chosen a target, and the record shows they chose.

shadow.fails: ⚠️ COLLAPSES INWARD — the harbor folds and everything sheltered inside is gone with it
shadow.counterplay: empty it first; the cost of the umbral vessel is that its failure kills what it was protecting
shadow.plainly: When it bursts, the harbor folds. Everyone and everything sheltered inside it is gone — not damaged, GONE, removed from play with no body. The bearer survives, standing where the harbor was.

appetite.fails: COLLECTS — the debt comes due against the bearer, at the price they set for others
appetite.plainly: When it bursts, every bargain the bearer holds comes due at once, against the bearer, at whatever price they set for the other party.

theDesignRule: ⚠️ A VESSEL'S OVERCHARGE MUST BE THE TRADITION'S OWN NIGHTMARE, not a generic explosion. The light one hurts everyone who can see. The shadow one kills what you were protecting. The living one grows into you. If two traditions' vessels fail the same way, one of them is authored wrong.
clarityNote: ⚠️ ADDED AFTER ERIK CAUGHT 'stand next to something else alive — a horrible decision to have to make' as vague, HOURS AFTER I amended DIRECTIVE_SNG-306 to cover my own writing. It was evocative and it specified nothing: not the damage, not how the target is chosen, not whether a plant counts. Every overcharge now carries a `plainly` alongside its evocative line — the same twin rule the crafts get. The tell was that I wrote the CONSEQUENCE ('a horrible decision') instead of the RULE ('the nearest living creature, ties toward the bearer').
